claim: Strong gamma-band oscillations in primate early visual cortex can be induced by homogeneous color surfaces.
source: Strong gamma-band oscillations in primate early visual cortex can be induced by homogeneous color surfaces (Peter et al., 2019; Shirhatti and Ray, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Peter et al., 2019; Shirhatti and Ray, 2018).

claim: Particularly strong gamma oscillations have been reported for red stimuli compared to other hues.
source: Compared to other hues, particularly strong gamma oscillations have been reported for red stimuli.
evidence: Supported by citations in the manuscript to previous reports (Bartoli et al., 2019; Li et al., 2022; Perry et al., 2020; Rols et al., 2001; Shirhatti and Ray, 2018).

claim: Precortical color processing and the resultant strength of input to V1 have often not been fully controlled for in previous studies.
source: However, precortical color processing and the resultant strength of input to V1 have often not been fully controlled for.
evidence: This is an inference based on the authors' review of previous literature and their motivation for the current study.

claim: Stronger responses to red might be due to differences in V1 input strength.
source: Therefore, stronger responses to red might be due to differences in V1 input strength.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis proposed by the authors to explain previous findings.

claim: The study presented stimuli that had equal luminance and cone contrast levels in a color coordinate system based on responses of the lateral geniculate nucleus.
source: We presented stimuli that had equal luminance and cone contrast levels in a color coordinate system based on responses of the lateral geniculate nucleus, the main input source for area V1.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and methods used in the study.

claim: The study recorded magnetoencephalography in 30 human participants.
source: With these stimuli, we recorded magnetoencephalography in 30 human participants.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods and sample size.

claim: Gamma oscillations were found in early visual cortex which did not differ between red and green stimuli of equal L-M cone contrast.
source: We found gamma oscillations in early visual cortex which, contrary to previous reports, did not differ between red and green stimuli of equal L-M cone contrast.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: Blue stimuli with contrast exclusively on the S-cone axis induced very weak gamma responses.
source: Notably, blue stimuli with contrast exclusively on the S-cone axis induced very weak gamma responses, as well as smaller event-related fields and poorer change-detection performance.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: Blue stimuli with contrast exclusively on the S-cone axis induced smaller event-related fields.
source: Notably, blue stimuli with contrast exclusively on the S-cone axis induced very weak gamma responses, as well as smaller event-related fields and poorer change-detection performance.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: Blue stimuli with contrast exclusively on the S-cone axis induced poorer change-detection performance.
source: Notably, blue stimuli with contrast exclusively on the S-cone axis induced very weak gamma responses, as well as smaller event-related fields and poorer change-detection performance.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: The strength of human color gamma responses for stimuli on the L-M axis could be well explained by L-M cone contrast.
source: The strength of human color gamma responses for stimuli on the L-M axis could be well explained by L-M cone contrast and did not show a clear red bias when L-M cone contrast was properly equalized.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Human color gamma responses for stimuli on the L-M axis did not show a clear red bias when L-M cone contrast was properly equalized.
source: The strength of human color gamma responses for stimuli on the L-M axis could be well explained by L-M cone contrast and did not show a clear red bias when L-M cone contrast was properly equalized.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Visual stimuli often induce rhythmic activity in the gamma band in early visual cortex of human and non-human primates.
source: In early visual cortex of human and non-human primates, visual stimuli often induce rhythmic activity in the gamma band (Hoogenboom et al., 2006; Jia et al., 2011; Kreiter and Singer, 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Gamma oscillations and their coherence between neuronal populations have been related to attentional selection.
source: Gamma oscillations and their coherence between neuronal populations have been related to attentional selection (Bauer et al., 2006; Bosman et al., 2012; Fries et al., 2001; Magazzini and Singh, 2018), directed information flow (Bastos et al., 2015; Besserve et al., 2015; Michalareas et al., 2016; van Kerkoerle et al., 2014), stimulus learning (Brunet et al., 2014; Peter et al., 2021; Stauch et al., 2021), and further cognitive functions (for reviews, see Fries, 2015; Singer, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Gamma oscillations and their coherence between neuronal populations have been related to directed information flow.
source: Gamma oscillations and their coherence between neuronal populations have been related to attentional selection (Bauer et al., 2006; Bosman et al., 2012; Fries et al., 2001; Magazzini and Singh, 2018), directed information flow (Bastos et al., 2015; Besserve et al., 2015; Michalareas et al., 2016; van Kerkoerle et al., 2014), stimulus learning (Brunet et al., 2014; Peter et al., 2021; Stauch et al., 2021), and further cognitive functions (for reviews, see Fries, 2015; Singer, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Gamma oscillations and their coherence between neuronal populations have been related to stimulus learning.
source: Gamma oscillations and their coherence between neuronal populations have been related to attentional selection (Bauer et al., 2006; Bosman et al., 2012; Fries et al., 2001; Magazzini and Singh, 2018), directed information flow (Bastos et al., 2015; Besserve et al., 2015; Michalareas et al., 2016; van Kerkoerle et al., 2014), stimulus learning (Brunet et al., 2014; Peter et al., 2021; Stauch et al., 2021), and further cognitive functions (for reviews, see Fries, 2015; Singer, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Especially strong gamma oscillations have been observed for high-contrast black and white stimuli that extend beyond the size of single-neuron receptive fields.
source: Especially strong gamma oscillations have been observed for high-contrast black and white stimuli that extend beyond the size of single-neuron receptive fields (Gieselmann and Thiele, 2008; Jia et al., 2011) and whose features are contiguous over space (Brunet and Fries, 2019; Hermes et al., 2019; Lowet et al., 2017; Uran et al., 2022; Vinck and Bosman, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Especially strong gamma oscillations have been observed for stimuli whose features are contiguous over space.
source: Especially strong gamma oscillations have been observed for high-contrast black and white stimuli that extend beyond the size of single-neuron receptive fields (Gieselmann and Thiele, 2008; Jia et al., 2011) and whose features are contiguous over space (Brunet and Fries, 2019; Hermes et al., 2019; Lowet et al., 2017; Uran et al., 2022; Vinck and Bosman, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Extensive and uniform stimuli synchronize larger populations of neurons into a common gamma rhythm, thereby generating a clearer oscillatory population signal.
source: Likely, this dependence exists because extensive and uniform stimuli synchronize larger populations of neurons into a common gamma rhythm, thereby generating a clearer oscillatory population signal (Gray et al., 1989; Lowet et al., 2015; Lowet et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Large homogeneous patches of color have been shown to induce strong gamma oscillations in the early visual cortex of macaques.
source: Large homogeneous patches of color have also been shown to induce strong gamma oscillations, both in the early visual cortex of macaques (Brunet et al., 2015; Peter et al., 2019; Rols et al., 2001; Shirhatti and Ray, 2018) and humans (Bartoli et al., 2019; Li et al., 2022; Perry et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Large homogeneous patches of color have been shown to induce strong gamma oscillations in the early visual cortex of humans.
source: Large homogeneous patches of color have also been shown to induce strong gamma oscillations, both in the early visual cortex of macaques (Brunet et al., 2015; Peter et al., 2019; Rols et al., 2001; Shirhatti and Ray, 2018) and humans (Bartoli et al., 2019; Li et al., 2022; Perry et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Red stimuli have been reported to induce especially strong gamma-band responses in several reports.
source: Interestingly, red stimuli have been reported to induce especially strong gamma-band responses in several of these reports (Bartoli et al., 2019; Li et al., 2022; Perry et al., 2020; Rols et al., 2001; Shirhatti and Ray, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: It has been speculated that stronger gamma responses to red might be due to a higher ecological relevance of the color red in natural environments.
source: It has been speculated that this might be due to a higher ecological relevance of the color red in natural environments (Bartoli et al., 2020), and it was recently related to potentially faster adaptation of the M-cone pathway (Peter et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis from previous literature, supported by citations.

claim: Stronger gamma responses to red were recently related to potentially faster adaptation of the M-cone pathway.
source: It has been speculated that this might be due to a higher ecological relevance of the color red in natural environments (Bartoli et al., 2020), and it was recently related to potentially faster adaptation of the M-cone pathway (Peter et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from previous literature, supported by citation.

claim: Gamma-power scales with the strength of excitatory synaptic input.
source: However, when comparing across different stimuli, the strength of input to the neuronal populations generating the investigated gamma signal should be controlled, because gamma-power scales with the strength of excitatory synaptic input (Hadjipapas et al., 2015; Henrie and Shapley, 2005; Lewis et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Color-induced gamma has mostly been studied in area V1.
source: Color-induced gamma has mostly been studied in area V1 (see above).
evidence: This is an inference based on the authors' review of previous literature.

claim: In primates, feedforward driving input to V1 originates mostly from the LGN.
source: In primates, feedforward driving input to V1 originates mostly from the LGN (Felleman and Van Essen, 1991; Sherman, 2005), including for color stimuli (Chatterjee and Callaway, 2003; Shapley, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In awake primates, the LGN itself does not show visually induced gamma.
source: Note that in awake primates, the LGN itself does not show visually induced gamma (Bastos et al., 2014; tested with grating stimuli), such that V1 is likely the first stage in the primate visual system generating gamma.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: V1 is likely the first stage in the primate visual system generating gamma.
source: Note that in awake primates, the LGN itself does not show visually induced gamma (Bastos et al., 2014; tested with grating stimuli), such that V1 is likely the first stage in the primate visual system generating gamma.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited evidence about LGN not showing gamma.

claim: LGN responses to color stimuli can be well explained by measuring retinal cone absorption spectra and constructing cone contrast axes: L+M, L-M, and S-(L+M).
source: Earlier work has established in the non-human primate that LGN responses to color stimuli can be well explained by measuring retinal cone absorption spectra and constructing the following cone contrast axes: L+M (capturing luminance), L-M (capturing redness vs. greenness), and S-(L+M) (capturing S-cone activation, which corresponds to violet vs. yellow hues).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work, as indicated by the phrase 'Earlier work has established'.

claim: The cone contrast axes L+M, L-M, and S-(L+M) span a color space referred to as DKL space.
source: These axes span a color space referred to as DKL space (Derrington et al., 1984).
evidence: Supported by citation to the original work defining DKL space.

claim: The DKL space insight from non-human primates can be translated to humans if one assumes that human LGN responses have a similar dependence on human cone responses.
source: This insight can be translated to humans (for recent examples, see Olkkonen et al., 2008; Witzel and Gegenfurtner, 2018), if one assumes that human LGN responses have a similar dependence on human cone responses.
evidence: This is an inference based on an assumption, supported by citations to recent examples.

claim: Recordings of human LGN single units to colored stimuli are not available.
source: Recordings of human LGN single units to colored stimuli are not available (to our knowledge).
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of data in the literature, based on the authors' knowledge.

claim: Sensitivity spectra of human retinal cones have been determined by ex vivo retinal unit recordings.
source: Yet, sensitivity spectra of human retinal cones have been determined by a number of approaches, including ex vivo retinal unit recordings (Schnapf et al., 1987), and psychophysical color matching (Stockman and Sharpe, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Sensitivity spectra of human retinal cones have been determined by psychophysical color matching.
source: Yet, sensitivity spectra of human retinal cones have been determined by a number of approaches, including ex vivo retinal unit recordings (Schnapf et al., 1987), and psychophysical color matching (Stockman and Sharpe, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Spectral peaks of cone opsin sensitivity show variability over individuals.
source: Because spectral peaks of cone opsin sensitivity show variability over individuals (Neitz and Jacobs, 1986; Neitz and Neitz, 2011), recruiting a larger sample than is possible in human patient or macaque studies is necessary to measure the general, population-wide relationship between stimulus color and induced gamma oscillations in the early visual cortex.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Recruiting a larger sample than is possible in human patient or macaque studies is necessary to measure the general, population-wide relationship between stimulus color and induced gamma oscillations in the early visual cortex.
source: Because spectral peaks of cone opsin sensitivity show variability over individuals (Neitz and Jacobs, 1986; Neitz and Neitz, 2011), recruiting a larger sample than is possible in human patient or macaque studies is necessary to measure the general, population-wide relationship between stimulus color and induced gamma oscillations in the early visual cortex.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited variability in cone opsin sensitivity.

claim: The study presented uniform, circular color disks picked from a DKL equiluminance plane on an equiluminant background.
source: In this study, we recorded MEG in 30 human participants while presenting them with uniform, circular color disks picked from a DKL equiluminance plane on an equiluminant background.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and methods.

claim: The cone contrasts of the stimuli on the L-M and the S-(L+M) axes were equalized.
source: Crucially, their cone contrasts on the L-M and the S-(L+M) axes were equalized.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and methods.

claim: The MEG recordings were analyzed at the source level.
source: We analyzed the MEG recordings at the source level (Gross et al., 2001; Van Veen et al., 1997) and found that color-induced gamma-band responses localized to early visual cortex with a peak in area V1, confirming that color gamma responses can be studied non-invasively in humans.
evidence: This describes the analysis methods used, supported by citations.

claim: Color-induced gamma-band responses localized to early visual cortex with a peak in area V1.
source: We analyzed the MEG recordings at the source level (Gross et al., 2001; Van Veen et al., 1997) and found that color-induced gamma-band responses localized to early visual cortex with a peak in area V1, confirming that color gamma responses can be studied non-invasively in humans.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: Color gamma responses can be studied non-invasively in humans.
source: We analyzed the MEG recordings at the source level (Gross et al., 2001; Van Veen et al., 1997) and found that color-induced gamma-band responses localized to early visual cortex with a peak in area V1, confirming that color gamma responses can be studied non-invasively in humans.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: With colors that had identical luminance and identical color contrast in DKL space, the study could not confirm stronger gamma responses for red stimuli.
source: With colors that had identical luminance and identical color contrast in DKL space, we could not confirm stronger gamma responses for red stimuli.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: Equiluminant colors with comparable absolute cone contrasts on the L-M axis induced gamma-power responses of equal strength in area V1, independent of their redness.
source: Instead, equiluminant colors with comparable absolute cone contrasts on the L-M axis induced gamma-power responses of equal strength in area V1, independent of their redness.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: Colors on the S-(L+M) axis induced weaker gamma power, especially for colors strongly activating only the S-cone.
source: Colors on the S-(L+M) axis induced weaker gamma power, especially for colors strongly activating only the S-cone.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: Participants' report accuracy was close to 85%.
source: As set by the staircase, participants' report accuracy was close to 85% (grating: 83%, CI95% = [76–87%], colors: 87%, CI95% = [86–87%], all confidence intervals based on nonparametric bootstraps).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: Change-detection performance differed across hues.
source: However, change-detection performance, as defined by the color contrast of the stimulus change on which the per-color staircases converged, differed across hues (F(7,203) = 82.18, p < 3 × 10−16).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support.

claim: Participants reached 85% accuracy with a change color contrast toward background between 20% for red-yellow and 37% for red-blue stimuli.
source: Participants reached 85% accuracy with a change color contrast toward background between 20% (CI95% = [17%, 23%]) for red-yellow and 37% (CI95% = [31%, 45%]) for red-blue stimuli (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data, also shown in Figure 2D.

claim: For blue stimuli, the necessary change color contrast toward background was 71%, significantly higher than for other hues.
source: There was one notable outlier: For blue stimuli, the necessary change color contrast toward background was 71% (CI95% = [66%, 76%]), significantly higher than for other hues (t(29) = 18.01, p < 3 × 10−16).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support.

claim: Participants took on average 496 ms to report the change location on grating stimuli.
source: On average, participants took 496 ms (CI95% = [467 ms, 524 ms]) to report the change location on grating stimuli.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: For color stimuli, participants took on average 547 ms to report the change location.
source: For color stimuli, they took on average 547 ms (CI95% = [521 ms, 570 ms]).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: Across the different color hues, reaction times differed.
source: Across the different color hues, reaction times differed (F(7,203) = 9.26, p < 7 × 10−10).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support.

claim: Subjects were quickest to detect contrast changes on red stimuli.
source: Subjects were quickest to detect contrast changes on red stimuli (mean = 509 ms, CI95% = [483 ms, 540 ms]), and slowest for green-yellow stimuli (mean = 562 ms, CI95% = [535 ms, 587 ms], Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data, also shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Subjects were slowest to detect contrast changes on green-yellow stimuli.
source: Subjects were quickest to detect contrast changes on red stimuli (mean = 509 ms, CI95% = [483 ms, 540 ms]), and slowest for green-yellow stimuli (mean = 562 ms, CI95% = [535 ms, 587 ms], Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data, also shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Both grating stimuli and equiluminant color disks induced clear visual event-related fields (ERFs) in area V1.
source: Both grating stimuli and equiluminant color disks induced clear visual event-related fields (ERFs) in area V1 (Figure 2A), with a shape and timing similar to visually evoked potentials recorded in macaque V1 (Figure 5B in Rols et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data, shown in Figure 2A and compared to previous work.

claim: The ERF differed across stimuli during a prominent component, 57- to 94-ms poststimulus onset.
source: The ERF differed across stimuli during a prominent component, 57- to 94-ms poststimulus onset (Figure 2B, F(3.48, 101.04) = 30.32, pGG < 3 × 10−15), which we suspect to be of similar origin as the N70 component recorded in Rols et al., 2001.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support, shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The N70 component was stronger for grating compared to color stimuli.
source: The N70 component was stronger for grating compared to color stimuli (Figure 2C) and t(9) = 6.80, p < 2 × 10−7).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support, shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Across stimulus hues, the N70 component was strongest for red and green-yellow stimuli.
source: Across stimulus hues, the N70 component was strongest for red (mean = −0.83, CI95% = [−0.96, −0.71]) and green-yellow stimuli (mean = −0.82, CI95% = [−0.94, −0.70]), and weakest for blue stimuli (mean = −0.33, CI95% = [−0.38, −0.29]).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: Across stimulus hues, the N70 component was weakest for blue stimuli.
source: Across stimulus hues, the N70 component was strongest for red (mean = −0.83, CI95% = [−0.96, −0.71]) and green-yellow stimuli (mean = −0.82, CI95% = [−0.94, −0.70]), and weakest for blue stimuli (mean = −0.33, CI95% = [−0.38, −0.29]).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: The per-participant, per-color N70 initial slope showed significant differences across hues.
source: We extracted the per-participant, per-color N70 initial slope and found significant differences across hues (F (4.89, 141.68) = 7.53, pGG < 4 × 10−6).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support.

claim: The N70 initial slope was shallower for blue hues compared to all other hues except for green and green-blue.
source: Specifically, it was shallower for blue hues compared to all other hues (all pHolm < 7 × 10−4) except for green and green-blue, while it was not significantly different between all other stimulus hue pairs (all pHolm > 0.07, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), demonstrating that stimulus drive (as estimated by ERF slope) was approximately equalized over all hues but blue.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Stimulus drive (as estimated by ERF slope) was approximately equalized over all hues but blue.
source: Specifically, it was shallower for blue hues compared to all other hues (all pHolm < 7 × 10−4) except for green and green-blue, while it was not significantly different between all other stimulus hue pairs (all pHolm > 0.07, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), demonstrating that stimulus drive (as estimated by ERF slope) was approximately equalized over all hues but blue.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The peak time of the N70 component was significantly later for blue stimuli compared to all but yellow, green, and green-yellow stimuli.
source: The peak time of the N70 component was significantly later for blue stimuli (mean = 88.6 ms, CI95% = [84.9 ms, 92.1 ms]) compared to all (all pHolm < 0.02) but yellow, green, and green-yellow stimuli, for yellow (mean = 84.4 ms, CI95% = [81.6 ms, 87.6 ms]) compared to red and red-blue stimuli (all pHolm < 0.03), and fastest for red stimuli (mean = 77.9 ms, CI95% = [74.5 ms, 81.1 ms]) showing a general pattern of slower N70 peaks for stimuli on the S-(L+M) axis, especially for blue (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The N70 peak time was fastest for red stimuli.
source: The peak time of the N70 component was significantly later for blue stimuli (mean = 88.6 ms, CI95% = [84.9 ms, 92.1 ms]) compared to all (all pHolm < 0.02) but yellow, green, and green-yellow stimuli, for yellow (mean = 84.4 ms, CI95% = [81.6 ms, 87.6 ms]) compared to red and red-blue stimuli (all pHolm < 0.03), and fastest for red stimuli (mean = 77.9 ms, CI95% = [74.5 ms, 81.1 ms]) showing a general pattern of slower N70 peaks for stimuli on the S-(L+M) axis, especially for blue (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: There is a general pattern of slower N70 peaks for stimuli on the S-(L+M) axis, especially for blue.
source: The peak time of the N70 component was significantly later for blue stimuli (mean = 88.6 ms, CI95% = [84.9 ms, 92.1 ms]) compared to all (all pHolm < 0.02) but yellow, green, and green-yellow stimuli, for yellow (mean = 84.4 ms, CI95% = [81.6 ms, 87.6 ms]) compared to red and red-blue stimuli (all pHolm < 0.03), and fastest for red stimuli (mean = 77.9 ms, CI95% = [74.5 ms, 81.1 ms]) showing a general pattern of slower N70 peaks for stimuli on the S-(L+M) axis, especially for blue (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Color and grating stimuli induced significant visual narrowband gamma-band power increases in early visual cortex.
source: In addition, color and grating stimuli induced significant visual narrowband gamma-band power increases in early visual cortex (Figure 3A–D, G, H).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data, shown in Figure 3A–D, G, H.

claim: Color stimuli induced gamma-power increases at the subject-specific gamma peak of on average 19% relative to the baseline.
source: Color stimuli induced gamma-power increases at the subject-specific gamma peak of on average 19% (CI95% = [14–26%]) relative to the baseline, whereas grating stimuli induced gamma-power increases of 100% (CI95% = [80–120%], tdifference(29) = 8.32, p < 4 × 10−9).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support.

claim: Grating stimuli induced gamma-power increases of 100% relative to the baseline.
source: Color stimuli induced gamma-power increases at the subject-specific gamma peak of on average 19% (CI95% = [14–26%]) relative to the baseline, whereas grating stimuli induced gamma-power increases of 100% (CI95% = [80–120%], tdifference(29) = 8.32, p < 4 × 10−9).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support.

claim: Grating- and color-induced gamma source-localized to similar sources, being strongest in areas V1/V2 and extending into parietal and temporal cortex.
source: Grating- and color-induced gamma source-localized to similar sources, being strongest in areas V1/V2 and extending into parietal and temporal cortex (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data, shown in Figure 3H.

claim: For both grating and color stimuli, induced gamma-power changes were strongest in areas V1, V2, V3, and V4.
source: For both grating and color stimuli, induced gamma-power changes were strongest in areas V1 (grating: 142%; color: 21%), V2 (grating: 131%, color: 19%), V3 (grating: 113%, color: 19%), and V4 (grating: 91%, color: 17%), respectively.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: Ninety-seven percent of all participants showed a significant gamma peak for at least one color and for the grating stimulus.
source: Ninety-seven percent of all participants showed a significant gamma peak for at least one color and for the grating stimulus.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: A second, higher gamma peak was detected in 90% of participants for at least one color stimulus.
source: A second, higher gamma peak was detected in 90% of participants for at least one color stimulus.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: Only 13% of participants showed a second gamma peak when the grating stimulus was shown.
source: While induced gamma was five times stronger for grating compared to color stimuli, only 13% of participants showed a second gamma peak when the grating stimulus was shown.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: For the two peaks often observed with color stimuli, there was no linear relation between the two fitted peak frequencies across colors and participants.
source: For the two peaks often observed with color stimuli, there was no linear relation between the two fitted peak frequencies across colors and participants (r = 0.06, p = 0.58, Figure 3F), indicating that the second peak was unlikely to be a harmonic of the first.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support, shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The second gamma peak was unlikely to be a harmonic of the first.
source: For the two peaks often observed with color stimuli, there was no linear relation between the two fitted peak frequencies across colors and participants (r = 0.06, p = 0.58, Figure 3F), indicating that the second peak was unlikely to be a harmonic of the first.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: There was a significant difference between the average lower gamma-peak frequencies induced by grating and color stimuli.
source: There was a significant difference between the average lower gamma-peak frequencies induced by grating (51.6 Hz, CI95% = [49.4 Hz, 53.7 Hz]) and color stimuli (45.9 Hz, CI95% = [42.6 Hz, 49.1 Hz], pdifference < 3 × 10−3).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support.

claim: Across participants, the gamma-peak frequencies induced by grating and by color stimuli were correlated.
source: Across participants, the gamma-peak frequencies induced by grating and by color stimuli were correlated (r = 0.64, p < 3 × 10−4).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support.

claim: None of the different color pairs showed significantly differing peak frequencies in pairwise comparisons within participants across different colors.
source: However, none of the different color pairs showed significantly differing peak frequencies in pairwise comparisons within participants across different colors (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, all pHolm > 0.36), also indicating that input drive was roughly equalized across colors (Lewis et al., 2021; Ray and Maunsell, 2010; Roberts et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Input drive was roughly equalized across colors.
source: However, none of the different color pairs showed significantly differing peak frequencies in pairwise comparisons within participants across different colors (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, all pHolm > 0.36), also indicating that input drive was roughly equalized across colors (Lewis et al., 2021; Ray and Maunsell, 2010; Roberts et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data, supported by citations.

claim: The higher gamma peak did not differ in peak frequencies induced by grating and color stimuli.
source: The higher peak did not differ in peak frequencies induced by grating (96.5 Hz, CI95% = [91.8 Hz, 101.3 Hz]) and color stimuli (97.1 Hz, CI95% = [95.0 Hz, 99.1 Hz], pDifference = 0.68) and showed no significant differences in pairwise comparisons across different colors (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D all pHolm > 0.37).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: For the red and green stimuli that were chosen to have equal absolute L-M contrast, the induced gamma-power change was not statistically different between the two.
source: Crucially, for the red and green stimuli that were chosen to have equal absolute L-M contrast, the induced gamma-power change was not statistically different between the two (Figure 3E, red: 30.8%, CI95% = [20.3%, 43.5%], green: 31.2%, CI95% = [21.2%, 42.2%], t(29) = 0.135, pHolm = 0.89, BF01 = 7.0).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data with statistical support, shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The data are 7.0 times more likely to occur under a hypothesis of no differences between red and green stimuli compared to a hypothesis assuming differences.
source: The Bayes factor can be interpreted as meaning that the data are 7.0 times more likely to occur under a hypothesis of no differences between red and green stimuli compared to a hypothesis assuming differences.
evidence: This is a statistical interpretation of the Bayes factor from the experimental data.

claim: On the S-(L+M) axis, stimuli with equal absolute cone contrasts showed differing induced gamma power.
source: On the S-(L+M) axis, stimuli with equal absolute cone contrasts showed differing induced gamma power: While yellow stimuli induced a 15.4% gamma-power increase over baseline (CI95% = [10.7%, 21.9%]), blue stimuli showed significantly smaller, very weak increases of only 2.2% (CI95% = [0.3%, 4.3%], t(29) = 4.02, pdifference < 0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support.

claim: Yellow stimuli induced a 15.4% gamma-power increase over baseline.
source: On the S-(L+M) axis, stimuli with equal absolute cone contrasts showed differing induced gamma power: While yellow stimuli induced a 15.4% gamma-power increase over baseline (CI95% = [10.7%, 21.9%]), blue stimuli showed significantly smaller, very weak increases of only 2.2% (CI95% = [0.3%, 4.3%], t(29) = 4.02, pdifference < 0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: Blue stimuli showed significantly smaller, very weak increases of only 2.2% gamma power over baseline.
source: On the S-(L+M) axis, stimuli with equal absolute cone contrasts showed differing induced gamma power: While yellow stimuli induced a 15.4% gamma-power increase over baseline (CI95% = [10.7%, 21.9%]), blue stimuli showed significantly smaller, very weak increases of only 2.2% (CI95% = [0.3%, 4.3%], t(29) = 4.02, pdifference < 0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support.

claim: After regressing out per participant, per color, the N70 slope and amplitude from the induced gamma power, the induced gamma-power change residuals were not statistically different between red and green stimuli.
source: To attempt to control for potential remaining differences in input drive that the DKL normalization missed, we regressed out per participant, per color, the N70 slope and amplitude from the induced gamma power. Results remained equivalent along the L-M axis: The induced gamma-power change residuals were not statistically different between red and green stimuli (red: 8.22, CI95% = [−0.42, 16.85], green: 12.09, CI95% = [5.44, 18.75], t(29) = 1.35, pHolm = 1.0, BF01 = 3.00).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support.

claim: Lower levels of input drive generated by equicontrast blue versus yellow stimuli might explain the weaker gamma oscillations induced by them.
source: While blue stimuli still showed weaker gamma-power change residuals than yellow stimuli when regressing out changes in N70 slope and amplitude (blue: −11.23, CI95% = [−16.89, −5.57], yellow: −6.35, CI95% = [−11.20, −1.50]), this difference did not reach significance (t(29) = 1.65, pHolm = 0.88). This suggests that lower levels of input drive generated by equicontrast blue versus yellow stimuli might explain the weaker gamma oscillations induced by them.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Higher change-detection performance was correlated with stronger average V1 dipole moment across colors, in the time period from 67- to 93-ms poststimulus onset.
source: Higher change-detection performance (defined as lower final staircased target color contrast) was correlated with stronger average V1 dipole moment (i.e., the negative ERF amplitude during the N70 component) across colors, in the time period from 67- to 93-ms poststimulus onset (Figure 4A, rmax = 0.43, all pTmax < 0.03, corrected for multiple comparisons across time).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support, shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Higher change-detection performance was correlated with stronger induced V1 power across colors, for several gamma frequency ranges.
source: Higher change-detection performance was also correlated with stronger induced V1 power across colors, for several gamma frequency ranges (Figure 4B; at 34–37 Hz: rmax = −0.27, all pTmax ≤ 0.03; at 39–40 Hz: rmax = −0.23, all pTmax < 0.04; at 44–53 Hz: rmax = −0.31, all pTmax ≤ 0.03, corrected for multiple comparisons across frequency).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support, shown in Figure 4B.

claim: There were significant correlations between the N70 ERF component and induced gamma power.
source: In addition, there were significant correlations between the N70 ERF component and induced gamma power: The extracted N70 amplitude was correlated across colors with the induced gamma-power change within participants with on average r = −0.38 (CI95% = [−0.49, −0.28], pWilcoxon < 4 × 10−6).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support.

claim: The correlation between N70 ERF component and induced gamma power was specific to the gamma band and the N70 component.
source: This correlation was specific to the gamma band and the N70 component: Across colors, there were significant correlation clusters between V1 dipole moment 68- to 79-ms poststimulus onset and induced power between 28–54 and 72 Hz (Figure 4C, rmax = −0.30, pTmax < 0.05, corrected for multiple comparisons across time and frequency).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support, shown in Figure 4C.

claim: When perceptual definitions of equiluminance are used, there is substantial between-subject variability in the ratio of relative L- and M-cone contributions to perceived luminance, with a mean ratio of L/M luminance contributions of 1.5–2.3.
source: When perceptual (instead of neuronal) definitions of equiluminance are used, there is substantial between-subject variability in the ratio of relative L- and M-cone contributions to perceived luminance, with a mean ratio of L/M luminance contributions of 1.5–2.3 (He et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The ratio of color change-detection performance between red and green (L divided by M) had an average value of 1.48, with substantial variability over subjects.
source: Our perceptual results are consistent with that: We had determined the color-contrast change-detection threshold per color; We used the inverse of this threshold as a metric of color change-detection performance; The ratio of this performance metric between red and green (L divided by M) had an average value of 1.48, with substantial variability over subjects (CI95% = [1.33, 1.66]).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: Change-detection threshold red/green ratios were neither correlated with ERF N70 amplitude red/green ratios nor with induced gamma-power red/green ratios.
source: If such variability also affected the neuronal ERF and gamma-power measures reported here, L/M-ratios in color-contrast change-detection thresholds should be correlated with L/M-ratios in ERF amplitude and induced gamma power across participants. This was not the case: Change-detection threshold red/green ratios were neither correlated with ERF N70 amplitude red/green ratios (ρ = 0.09, p = 0.65, BF01 = 3.99), nor with induced gamma-power red/green ratios (ρ = −0.17, p = 0.38, BF01 = 3.04).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support.

claim: Uniform colored stimuli induced gamma oscillations in humans that were measurable in MEG recordings, confirming a previous study.
source: In summary, uniform colored stimuli induced gamma oscillations in humans that were measurable in MEG recordings, confirming a previous study (Perry et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental data, supported by citation to previous study.

claim: When red-green color hues were chosen to equalize cone contrast on the L-M axis, the induced V1 gamma power did not differ between red and green hues.
source: When red-green color hues were chosen to equalize cone contrast on the L-M axis (and thereby to ideally equalize input drive), the induced V1 gamma power did not differ between red and green hues.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: Pure activation of the S-(L+M) axis induced weaker gamma power, especially for color hues activating primarily the S-cone.
source: Additionally, pure activation of the S-(L+M) axis induced weaker gamma power, especially for color hues activating primarily the S-cone.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: The asymmetry on the S-(L+M) axis could be seen in smaller amplitudes of early ERF components (N70) in area V1 and in worse color-contrast change-detection performance for high-S (blue) stimuli.
source: This curious asymmetry on the S-(L+M) axis could also be seen in smaller amplitudes of early ERF components (N70) in area V1 and in worse color-contrast change-detection performance for high-S (blue) stimuli.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Across hues, N70 amplitude and gamma power were correlated with color-contrast change-detection performance.
source: Accordingly, across hues, N70 amplitude and gamma power were correlated with color-contrast change-detection performance.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Controlling for N70 amplitude and slope strongly diminished the recorded differences in induced gamma power between S+ and S− stimuli.
source: The fact that controlling for N70 amplitude and slope strongly diminished the recorded differences in induced gamma power between S+ and S− stimuli supports the idea that the recorded differences in induced gamma power over the S-(L+M) axis might be due to pure S+ stimuli generating weaker input drive to V1 compared to DKL-equicontrast S− stimuli, even when cone contrasts are equalized.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The recorded differences in induced gamma power over the S-(L+M) axis might be due to pure S+ stimuli generating weaker input drive to V1 compared to DKL-equicontrast S− stimuli, even when cone contrasts are equalized.
source: The fact that controlling for N70 amplitude and slope strongly diminished the recorded differences in induced gamma power between S+ and S− stimuli supports the idea that the recorded differences in induced gamma power over the S-(L+M) axis might be due to pure S+ stimuli generating weaker input drive to V1 compared to DKL-equicontrast S− stimuli, even when cone contrasts are equalized.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The study found stronger gamma power and ERF N70 responses to stimuli along the green-yellow/red-blue axis compared to stimuli along the red-yellow/green-blue axis.
source: Concerning off-axis colors (red-blue, green-blue, green-yellow, and red-yellow), we found stronger gamma power and ERF N70 responses to stimuli along the green-yellow/red-blue axis (which has been called lime-magenta in previous studies) compared to stimuli along the red-yellow/green-blue axis (orange-cyan).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: In human studies varying color contrast along these axes, lime-magenta has been found to induce stronger fMRI responses.
source: In human studies varying color contrast along these axes, lime-magenta has also been found to induce stronger fMRI responses (Goddard et al., 2010; but see Lafer-Sousa et al., 2012), and psychophysical work has proposed a cortical color channel along this axis (Danilova and Mollon, 2010; but see Witzel and Gegenfurtner, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Psychophysical work has proposed a cortical color channel along the lime-magenta axis.
source: In human studies varying color contrast along these axes, lime-magenta has also been found to induce stronger fMRI responses (Goddard et al., 2010; but see Lafer-Sousa et al., 2012), and psychophysical work has proposed a cortical color channel along this axis (Danilova and Mollon, 2010; but see Witzel and Gegenfurtner, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The color-induced gamma oscillation clearly localized to early visual cortex, was narrow-banded and showed (for 90% of subjects) a second spectral peak around 80–100 Hz.
source: In our data, the color-induced gamma oscillation clearly localized to early visual cortex, was narrow-banded and showed (for 90% of subjects) a second spectral peak around 80–100 Hz, which did not seem to be a harmonic of the main induced peak and which was rare for grating stimuli.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: The second spectral peak did not seem to be a harmonic of the main induced peak and was rare for grating stimuli.
source: In our data, the color-induced gamma oscillation clearly localized to early visual cortex, was narrow-banded and showed (for 90% of subjects) a second spectral peak around 80–100 Hz, which did not seem to be a harmonic of the main induced peak and which was rare for grating stimuli.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: The induced gamma-power change source-localized as a continuous source over the early visual cortex with a peak in V1.
source: As the induced gamma-power change source-localized as a continuous source over the early visual cortex with a peak in V1, our data cannot differentiate between a strong gamma source in V1 that shows source smearing over neighboring areas and, alternatively, several gamma sources in V1–V4 that show monotonous decreases in power with distance from V1.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: The data cannot differentiate between a strong gamma source in V1 that shows source smearing over neighboring areas and several gamma sources in V1–V4 that show monotonous decreases in power with distance from V1.
source: As the induced gamma-power change source-localized as a continuous source over the early visual cortex with a peak in V1, our data cannot differentiate between a strong gamma source in V1 that shows source smearing over neighboring areas and, alternatively, several gamma sources in V1–V4 that show monotonous decreases in power with distance from V1.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors based on their data.

claim: Recruiting a bigger sample of human participants allowed the study to generalize findings of color gamma responses to the population level.
source: While most previous studies of gamma responses to colored stimuli were limited to small samples of non-human primates or human patients, recruiting a bigger sample of human participants allowed us to generalize findings of color gamma responses to the population level (Fries and Maris, 2022).
evidence: This is a methodological advantage claimed by the authors, supported by citation.

claim: The MEG signal does not represent a simple average over all population activity underneath the MEG sensor, but is influenced by the location and orientation of the underlying neuronal dipoles and is most sensitive to synchronized neuronal activity.
source: When comparing our results to previous reports based on intracranial recordings, it is important to note that the MEG signal does not represent a simple average over all population activity underneath the MEG sensor, but is influenced by the location and orientation of the underlying neuronal dipoles and is most sensitive to synchronized neuronal activity (Baillet, 2017; Murakami and Okada, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge about MEG, supported by citations.

claim: The total power reported in MEG does not correspond to the total power of all oscillatory neuronal activity in V1.
source: Thereby, the total power reported here does not correspond to the total power of all oscillatory neuronal activity in V1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of MEG signals.

claim: Activity sources that are of unequal frequency or phase are likely not fully captured in MEG recordings.
source: Additionally, activity sources that are of unequal frequency or phase are likely not fully captured in MEG recordings.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of MEG signals.

claim: Intracortical recordings will usually not sample all of area V1 equally, but will emphasize the color tuning of neuronal populations close to the electrodes.
source: On the other hand, intracortical recordings will usually not sample all of area V1 equally, but will emphasize the color tuning of neuronal populations close to the electrodes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of intracortical recordings.

claim: With careful head stabilization and exclusion of subjects showing excessive head movements, spatial resolution of source-localized MEG can be brought down to between 0.45 and 7 mm, depending on dipole location.
source: The localization accuracy of source-localized MEG is limited by subject movement, uncertainties in head tracking and source spread. However, with careful head stabilization and exclusion of subjects showing excessive head movements (as practiced here), spatial resolution can be brought down to between 0.45 and 7 mm, depending on dipole location (Nasiotis et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The high similarity between early (source-localized) V1 ERF components recorded in this study and intracortical V1 ERP components recorded in macaque suggests that V1-localized activity in MEG captures the underlying intracortical voltage signal in V1.
source: Additionally, the high similarity between early (source-localized) V1 ERF components recorded here and intracortical V1 ERP components recorded in macaque (Rols et al., 2001) suggests that our V1-localized activity in MEG captures the underlying intracortical voltage signal in V1.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with previous work, supported by citation.

claim: In most previous studies analyzing early visual cortex gamma-band responses to colored stimuli, the presented colors were not equiluminant and did not have equal color contrasts to the background.
source: In several previous studies in non-human and human primates analyzing early visual cortex gamma-band responses to colored stimuli, a red effect, that is stronger induced gamma power for red versus non-red colors, was reported. In most of these studies, the presented colors were not equiluminant and did not have equal color contrasts to the background.
evidence: This is an inference based on the authors' review of previous literature.

claim: Rols et al., 2001 described stronger gamma power for a red stimulus compared to a green and a yellow one in anesthetized macaque V1 and V4.
source: In an initial report on recordings in anesthetized macaque V1 and V4, Rols et al., 2001 first described stronger gamma power for a red stimulus compared to a green and a yellow one (heteroluminant, all presented on a gray background).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Color-induced gamma oscillations were significantly stronger in V1 than in V4 in the recordings by Rols et al., 2001.
source: Similar to our study, color-induced gamma oscillations were significantly stronger in V1 than in V4 in their recordings.
evidence: This is a comparison to previous work, supported by implicit citation.

claim: Shirhatti and Ray, 2018, recording in awake macaque V1, found strongest gamma power for red and blue hues.
source: Shirhatti and Ray, 2018, recording in awake macaque V1, presented fullscreen, heteroluminant colors after a gray intertrial background and found strongest gamma power for red and blue hues.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: When colors were transformed to coordinates based on L- and M-cone activation, induced gamma power was found to increase with cone contrast modulations toward both axis directions in one of the three monkeys tested by Shirhatti and Ray, 2018.
source: When colors were transformed to coordinates based on L- and M-cone activation, induced gamma power was found to increase with cone contrast modulations toward both axis directions in one of the three monkeys tested.
evidence: Supported by implicit citation to Shirhatti and Ray, 2018.

claim: Brunet et al., 2015 found that the strongest gamma power was induced by images of a colored orange on a gray background in ECoG recordings over awake macaque areas V1 and V4.
source: Using natural stimuli, Brunet et al., 2015 presented 65 grayscale and color images to two macaque monkeys and found that, in ECoG recordings over awake macaque areas V1 and V4, the strongest gamma power was induced by images of a colored orange on a gray background.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: In another study of macaque V1 responses to natural stimuli, induced gamma power increased with both negative and positive L-M cone contrast.
source: In another study of macaque V1 responses to natural stimuli, induced gamma power increased with both negative and positive L-M cone contrast (Peter et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Peter et al., 2019 found strongest gamma responses to pink and red stimuli in intracortical recordings from macaque V1 under visual stimulation with a peripheral colored disk.
source: In intracortical recordings from macaque V1 under visual stimulation with a peripheral colored disk, Peter et al., 2019 found strongest gamma responses to pink and red stimuli.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: When colors were chosen from an equiluminance plane in DKL space for a control analysis in one monkey, Peter et al., 2019 still found slightly stronger gamma power for red than for green stimuli, even if red and green stimuli were of the same color contrast.
source: When colors were chosen from an equiluminance plane in DKL space for a control analysis in one monkey, they still found slightly stronger gamma power for red than for green stimuli, even if red and green stimuli were of the same color contrast.
evidence: Supported by implicit citation to Peter et al., 2019.

claim: Peter et al., 2019 found the same asymmetry on the S-(L+M) axis as reported in the current study, in the sense that pure blue stimuli induced very weak gamma power.
source: The same asymmetry on the S-(L+M) axis as reported here was found, in the sense that pure blue stimuli induced very weak gamma power.
evidence: This is a comparison to previous work, supported by implicit citation to Peter et al., 2019.

claim: Peter et al., 2019 found that red induced the strongest gamma power only when presented on a gray background, but not when presented on a black background.
source: In addition, they explored the effects of prestimulus and background adaptation and found that red induced the strongest gamma power only when presented on a gray background, but not when presented on a black background.
evidence: Supported by implicit citation to Peter et al., 2019.

claim: Peter et al., 2019 showed that red and green stimuli induce equal gamma power when the background does not adapt M- and L-cones.
source: Presenting a series of different stimulus and background combinations and summarizing results in a self-defined cone adaptation model, they showed that red and green stimuli induce equal gamma power when the background does not adapt M- and L-cones, and that, over all stimulus/background combinations, M-cone-activating backgrounds boost L-cone-stimulus-driven gamma oscillations the strongest.
evidence: Supported by implicit citation to Peter et al., 2019.

claim: Peter et al., 2019 showed that M-cone-activating backgrounds boost L-cone-stimulus-driven gamma oscillations the strongest.
source: Presenting a series of different stimulus and background combinations and summarizing results in a self-defined cone adaptation model, they showed that red and green stimuli induce equal gamma power when the background does not adapt M- and L-cones, and that, over all stimulus/background combinations, M-cone-activating backgrounds boost L-cone-stimulus-driven gamma oscillations the strongest.
evidence: Supported by implicit citation to Peter et al., 2019.

claim: Bartoli et al., 2019 found strongest gamma-power responses for full-screen red/orange stimuli following a gray intertrial interval background in recordings from ECoG electrodes implanted over areas V1–V4 in 10 epilepsy patients.
source: In recordings from ECoG electrodes implanted over areas V1–V4 in 10 epilepsy patients, Bartoli et al., 2019 found strongest gamma-power responses for full-screen red/orange stimuli following a gray intertrial interval background.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The presented colors in Bartoli et al., 2019 were equiluminant and equicontrast in CIELAB, a color coordinate system based on perceptual similarity.
source: The presented colors were equiluminant and equicontrast in CIELAB, a color coordinate system based on perceptual similarity.
evidence: This describes the methods of a previous study, supported by implicit citation to Bartoli et al., 2019.

claim: In ECoG and intracranial EEG recordings from a second set of seven epilepsy patients using the same task and stimuli, Li et al., 2022 found strongest gamma-power responses for red/orange and green stimuli.
source: In ECoG and intracranial EEG recordings from a second set of seven epilepsy patients using the same task and stimuli (Li et al., 2022), strongest gamma-power responses were found for red/orange and green stimuli.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Color gamma responses reported in Bartoli et al., 2019 and Li et al., 2022 were of similar strength (expressed in percent change from baseline) as in the current MEG study.
source: Color gamma responses reported in both studies were of similar strength (expressed in percent change from baseline) as in our MEG study.
evidence: This is a comparison to previous work, supported by implicit citations.

claim: Perry et al., 2020 reported oscillatory neuronal responses to full-screen colored stimuli in MEG recordings from 20 participants.
source: Oscillatory neuronal responses to full-screen colored stimuli have also been reported in MEG recordings from 20 participants (Perry et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: When full-screen red, green, purple, and blue colors were shown after a gray background or in alteration, red stimuli induced the strongest power in several oscillatory bands above 30 Hz in Perry et al., 2020.
source: When full-screen red, green, purple, and blue colors were shown after a gray background or in alteration, red stimuli induced the strongest power in several oscillatory bands above 30 Hz.
evidence: Supported by implicit citation to Perry et al., 2020.

claim: All previous studies not explicitly controlling for cone contrast found stronger gamma-power responses for red (and sometimes blue) stimuli than for other colors.
source: In total, all previous studies not explicitly controlling for cone contrast found stronger gamma-power responses for red (and sometimes blue) stimuli than for other colors.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the authors' review of previous literature.

claim: When cone contrast was controlled for in two macaque V1 studies, the difference between red and green stimuli either decreased or disappeared.
source: When cone contrast was controlled for in two macaque V1 studies, either through the use of DKL coordinates or through a self-defined cone adaption model, the difference between red and green stimuli either decreased (Peter et al., 2019; Shirhatti and Ray, 2018) or, when adaptation was also taken into account, disappeared (Peter et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a summary of previous work, supported by citations.

claim: Macaque V1 glucose uptake, intrinsic signal imaging and 2-photon calcium imaging found strongest responses for the employed red and blue stimuli.
source: Interestingly, a similar case has been found before in other measures of V1 activation: Macaque V1 glucose uptake, intrinsic signal imaging and 2-photon calcium imaging found strongest responses for the employed red and blue stimuli (Garg et al., 2019; Li et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2020; Tootell et al., 1988; Xiao et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: End-spectral biases in V1 activation measures were likely at least partially an effect of the respective stimulus presentation and color coordinate systems.
source: These so-called end-spectral biases were likely at least partially an effect of the respective stimulus presentation and color coordinate systems, insofar as their red and blue colors induced maximal cone contrasts in the L-M pathway – highest L-M excitation for their red stimuli, and highest L excitation for their blue stimuli (Li et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2020; Mollon, 2009; Valverde Salzmann et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on previous work, supported by citations.

claim: Compared to L- and M-cones, S-cones are sparser.
source: This asymmetry on the S-(L+M) axis might be driven by underlying physiology: Compared to L- and M-cones, S-cones are sparser (DeMonasterio et al., 1981) and show slower light responses, higher noise levels, and higher activation thresholds (Baudin et al., 2019; Cole et al., 1993; Lee et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: S-cones show slower light responses, higher noise levels, and higher activation thresholds compared to L- and M-cones.
source: This asymmetry on the S-(L+M) axis might be driven by underlying physiology: Compared to L- and M-cones, S-cones are sparser (DeMonasterio et al., 1981) and show slower light responses, higher noise levels, and higher activation thresholds (Baudin et al., 2019; Cole et al., 1993; Lee et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: S-(L+M)-sensitive neurons are sparser than L-M-sensitive ones in the LGN.
source: Additionally, S-(L+M)-sensitive neurons are sparser than L-M-sensitive ones in the LGN (Derrington et al., 1984) and V1 (Li et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: S-(L+M)-sensitive neurons are sparser than L-M-sensitive ones in V1.
source: Additionally, S-(L+M)-sensitive neurons are sparser than L-M-sensitive ones in the LGN (Derrington et al., 1984) and V1 (Li et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Within V1, neurons sensitive to S-cone inputs reside in different cortical layers and respond later than other color-sensitive neurons.
source: Within V1, neurons sensitive to S-cone inputs reside in different cortical layers and respond later than other color-sensitive neurons (Cottaris and De Valois, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: S-cone-induced signals are comparatively weak within LGN and are amplified and transformed in V1.
source: Likely, S-cone-induced signals are comparatively weak within LGN and are amplified and transformed in V1 (De Valois et al., 2000; Mullen et al., 2008; Xiao, 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on previous work, supported by citations.

claim: Stimuli high and low on the S-(L+M) axis (S+ and S−) each target different cell populations in the LGN.
source: Contrary to the unified pathway for L-M activation, stimuli high and low on the S-(L+M) axis (S+ and S−) each target different cell populations in the LGN, and different cortical layers within V1 (Chatterjee and Callaway, 2003; De Valois et al., 2000), whereby the S+ pathway shows higher LGN neuron and V1 afferent input numbers (Chatterjee and Callaway, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Stimuli high and low on the S-(L+M) axis (S+ and S−) each target different cortical layers within V1.
source: Contrary to the unified pathway for L-M activation, stimuli high and low on the S-(L+M) axis (S+ and S−) each target different cell populations in the LGN, and different cortical layers within V1 (Chatterjee and Callaway, 2003; De Valois et al., 2000), whereby the S+ pathway shows higher LGN neuron and V1 afferent input numbers (Chatterjee and Callaway, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The S+ pathway shows higher LGN neuron and V1 afferent input numbers.
source: Contrary to the unified pathway for L-M activation, stimuli high and low on the S-(L+M) axis (S+ and S−) each target different cell populations in the LGN, and different cortical layers within V1 (Chatterjee and Callaway, 2003; De Valois et al., 2000), whereby the S+ pathway shows higher LGN neuron and V1 afferent input numbers (Chatterjee and Callaway, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: ERPs/ERFs reveal that more numerous S+ inputs result in a weaker evoked potential that also shows a longer latency.
source: Other metrics of V1 activation, such as ERPs/ERFs, reveal that these more numerous S+ inputs result in a weaker evoked potential that also shows a longer latency (our data; Nunez et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study and previous work, supported by citation.

claim: The results suggest that cortical gamma is more closely related to the processes reflected in the ERP/ERF.

claim: Color-induced gamma responses in area V1 match LGN-to-V1 input strength in three measured aspects.
source: In sum, color-induced gamma responses in area V1 match LGN-to-V1 input strength in three measured aspects: (1) along the L-M axis, stimuli driving LGN to an equal degree induce gamma oscillations that do not differ measurably in strength across the population; (2) gamma oscillations are strongly diminished for S-cone-driving stimuli, which are encoded by smaller populations of LGN neurons and which provide weaker excitatory input into V1, compared to L-M-cone-driving stimuli; (3) the amplitude of the early, input-driven N70 component is correlated with later induced gamma power over stimuli.
